q: The technician counts the lifejackets with you: eight for eight people. What do you ask for before you sign?
a: Two child lifejackets sized by weight, plus a spare adult one
o: Nothing — eight jackets for eight people is the rule
Two more adult jackets, straps pulled tight for the children
A note on the form that the children stay in the cockpit
why: One lifejacket per person of the right size, plus spares; an adult jacket slides straight off a child.

fig.title: Lifejackets, cockpit locker
lines: Crew list: 6 adults, 2 children (24 kg, 31 kg)

q: You open the cover of one inflatable lifejacket and find this. What do you do?
a: Ask the base to service or replace the jackets before you leave
o: Screw the cylinder home by hand and sign — the rest is cosmetic
Pull the toggle to prove it inflates, then sign the form
Accept them — a jacket is only serviced after it has been used
why: Loose cylinder, red indicator, overdue service: the jacket may not inflate. The base replaces it, you note it.

q: You plan an overnight passage to Kos. What do you do about this before you sign?
a: Ask for new webbing and a tether, rig the jackstays and test each clip
o: Leave them in the locker — the Dodecanese is coastal sailing
Rig them as they are; the webbing is only used in daylight
Run a mooring line along the deck instead and sign for them
why: You clip on at night and in a sea; faded webbing and a bent hook will not hold a fall.

fig.title: Harnesses and jackstays
lines: Stowed in the locker, not rigged

q: The technician says the liferaft 'is fine, nobody has ever opened it'. What do you do?
a: Refuse to sail until an in-date raft is aboard
o: Accept it — a raft is only serviced after inflation
Take it, but note the date on the form in case
Ask for a second raft to make up for the old one
why: A raft past its service date may not inflate; an expired raft means you do not leave the pontoon.

q: The raft is in date. You look at the cradle on the coachroof. What do you ask for before you sign?
a: An 8-person raft, painter made fast, padlock swapped for a quick-release
o: A second 6-person raft, with its painter tied to the first
The padlock key kept at the chart table, noted on the form
Nothing — six is enough: the dinghy takes the other two
why: Raft capacity covers everyone aboard; the painter is tied on, and the lashings open by hand or hydrostatic release.

fig.title: Liferaft in its cradle
lines: Painter: coiled in the cradle, not tied

q: You check the flares in the container against the base's list. What goes on the form?
a: In date: 0 parachute, 2 hand, 2 smoke — base to make up the list
o: 6 flares as counted — the dates are the base's responsibility
2 parachute, 2 hand, 2 smoke — the list is for bigger yachts
4 in date — expired flares still fire, only less reliably
why: Only in-date flares count; write the real count on the form and the base makes up the shortfall before departure.

q: You walk the boat with the base's list of fire gear. What do you ask for?
a: Aft cabin extinguisher replaced, one at the engine port, a fire blanket
o: Nothing — the galley extinguisher covers a 45 ft monohull
The aft cabin one shaken hard — settled powder lifts the gauge
A bucket on a lanyard by the galley instead of a blanket
why: Count, type, gauge in the green and service date per extinguisher; the engine port needs its own, the galley its blanket.

fig.title: Fire gear, base's list: 3 extinguishers
lines: Aft cabin: 1 kg powder, gauge red, 2022
Engine bay: fire port, no extinguisher beside it

q: The technician hands you a new fire blanket and asks where you want it. Where does it go?
a: By the galley, reachable without leaning over the stove
o: In the engine bay, next to the extinguisher port
In the forepeak, with the spare sails and the tools
In the cockpit locker, together with the flares
why: A blanket is for a pan or stove fire: mounted beside the galley, on the side away from the flames.

q: You press the EPIRB's test button and read the label. What do you do?
a: Ask for a replacement — battery expired, self-test fails
o: Write 'EPIRB tested' on the form — the light is just weak
Take it — in an emergency you would use the VHF first
Pull the sea switch to prove it transmits, then sign
why: Registration, battery date and a passed self-test are the three checks; a dead EPIRB is replaced, never 'tested live'.

fig.title: EPIRB, bracket by the companionway
lines: Registered: this yacht, MMSI on the label

q: You open the first-aid kit against the inventory list. What do you do?
a: List the missing and expired items on the form; the base restocks it
o: Sign — you will buy what you need at the pharmacy in town
Sign — a first-aid kit is a courtesy, not an inventory item
Take the whole kit ashore and bring your own instead
why: The kit is inventory: contents and dates are checked, shortfalls are written down and made up by the base.

q: At the pushpit the technician shows you the horseshoe. You picture this moment on Monday. What do you ask for?
a: The horseshoe on a quick-release clip, with a light and a danbuoy
o: The horseshoe lashed tighter so a sea cannot take it
A second horseshoe at the bow for a bow-first pick-up
Nothing — the fenders float and are quicker to throw
why: MOB gear goes in seconds: horseshoe and danbuoy on a quick release, a light for the night, a throwing line within reach.

fig.note: Horseshoe lashed on with a knot · no light · no danbuoy

q: The technician points at the emergency tiller under the bunk and moves on. What do you do?
a: Open the deck plate and fit it on the rudder stock yourself, now
o: Note where it is kept — fitting it is for an emergency
Ask the technician to confirm it fits, and sign
Lash it in the cockpit so it is ready when needed
why: Find it and try it: a tiller that does not fit, or a plate that will not open, is found at the base, not in a gale.

fig.title: Emergency tiller
lines: Found: under the aft cabin bunk
Rudder-stock plate: cockpit sole, aft of the wheel

q: You lift the floorboards with the technician and find this. What do you ask for?
a: A bung tied to each seacock and the manual pump handle
o: Nothing — the electric pump works and the bungs are aboard
A spare electric pump in place of the manual one
The bungs hammered into the seacocks now, to be ready
why: A bung lives tied to its seacock; the manual pump needs its handle in place — power is the first thing to go.

fig.title: Below the floorboards
lines: Bag of softwood bungs: chart table
Electric bilge pump: runs on test

q: This is what the safety locker holds against the base's list. What goes on the form?
a: Bolt cutters, a full foghorn and spare batteries — base to supply
o: Nothing — a knife, a phone light and AIS cover all of these
The foghorn only — the rest is for offshore boats
The bolt cutters only — the rest you can buy in town
why: Cutters or a rigging knife for a lost mast, a working horn, a torch with spares; the grab bag you pack yourself.

q: Two of your crew are weak swimmers. Before you leave you ask the technician how a person in the water gets back aboard. What answer do you want?
a: The bathing ladder drops from the water and a spare halyard reaches a cockpit winch to hoist someone up
o: The crew pull the casualty in over the guardrail together
The dinghy is launched and the casualty climbs into it
The liferaft is thrown to the casualty as a float
why: Recovery is planned at the base: a ladder that opens from the water and a halyard to a winch for someone who cannot climb; try both.

fig.title: Getting back aboard
lines: Bathing ladder: folds down from the platform
Spare halyard: topping lift to a cockpit winch

q: The base manager reads out the emergency numbers at the briefing. Where do they go?
a: On a card by the VHF and in your phone, before you leave
o: In the ship's log, to look up when they are needed
In the base's folder — it stays aboard anyway
In your head — three numbers are easy to remember
why: Channel 16, the base's phone and the local emergency number: written where any crew member can find them.

fig.title: Base briefing — numbers
lines: Base office: phone on the key fob

q: The technician shrugs: 'the lifebuoy light is extra, nobody checks it'. What do you do?
a: Ask for the light — the base's list is the law's minimum for the boat
o: Take his word for it — the base knows the local rules
Buy a light in town and claim it back from the deposit
Cross the light off the list before you sign the form
why: The base's list is the national equipment regulation for the flag; every item on it is aboard before you sign.

q: The raft cannot be swapped before Monday. What do you do?
a: Stay at the base until a serviced raft is aboard; note it on the form
o: Sail Sunday inside the Ionian and come back Monday for the raft
Sail with the dinghy inflated on deck in place of the raft
Sign for the boat and ask for a discount instead of a raft
why: Out-of-date safety gear is replaced before you leave; the base's problem does not become your crew's risk.

q: The boat is signed for and the crew are aboard. What do you do before supper?
a: Walk them through lifejackets, MOB, gas, heads and who does what
o: Let them settle in — the briefing is better once under way
Brief the two who have sailed; they pass it on to the rest
Show them the lifejackets; the rest is covered on the first sail
why: Your own safety briefing before leaving: jackets and where they are, MOB, gas and heads, swim rules, jobs.

q: The technician shows you the swim ladder. What rule do you set for your crew before anyone swims?
a: Engine off and key out, ladder down, then into the water
o: Engine in neutral, ticking over to charge the batteries
Engine off, ladder up so nobody climbs near the propeller
Lifejackets on for everyone who goes in the water
why: A turning propeller kills; a ladder down means a tired swimmer can get back aboard.
